question: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a near-lethal hanging attempt from which he was resuscitated. He has no current active suicidal ideation and his family is present and supportive. Which statement BEST reflects correct clinical reasoning for this patient?

answers.text: The absence of current active suicidal ideation means he can be safely discharged with outpatient follow-up.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reasoning is flawed. A prior near-lethal attempt is the single strongest predictor of future suicide — stronger than current ideation. The absence of stated ideation at a single assessment point should never override a history of high-lethality attempt. Disposition must account for the full risk profile.

answers.text: Because he attempted suicide, he has committed an offence under Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 and must be reported to the police.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is incorrect and harmful. Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act (MHCA) 2017 DECRIMINALISED suicide attempt in India — it replaced the earlier Indian Penal Code provision under the 1987 framework. The MHCA 2017 mandates that a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and must receive care, not criminal prosecution.

answers.text: His history of a near-lethal prior attempt is the single most important risk factor and warrants a comprehensive risk stratification before any disposition decision.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A prior attempt — especially one of high lethality — is the single strongest predictor of future suicide. Even with supportive family and absent current ideation, this patient requires comprehensive risk stratification, means restriction counselling, and a documented safety plan before disposition. Lethality of the prior attempt amplifies risk further.

answers.text: Family support and absence of ideation are strong protective factors that outweigh the prior attempt in this case.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Family support is a genuine protective factor, but it does not outweigh a near-lethal prior attempt in the risk calculus. Risk and protective factors must be weighed together — a near-lethal attempt shifts the risk stratum significantly and cannot be neutralised by a single protective factor alone.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key principles: (1) prior near-lethal attempt = strongest single predictor of future suicide; (2) MHCA 2017 Section 115 decriminalised suicide attempt in India — report to police is not only wrong but illegal; (3) protective factors reduce risk but do not nullify a high-lethality prior attempt.
Correct. Prior attempt lethality is the dominant predictor in this scenario, and the MHCA 2017 (Section 115) decriminalised suicide attempt — the clinician's role is care, not criminalisation.
